entries.3777a406f169d3aef2953ca0fe4d62b3501e69fd: <div sID="gen18992" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="30" osisID="Ezek.30" sID="Ezek.30"/> <div eID="gen18992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18993" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18994" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A continuation of the prophecy against Egypt, which we had in the latter part of the foregoing chapter, just before the desolation of that once flourishing kingdom was completed by Nebuchadnezzar, in which is foretold the destruction of all her allies and confederates, all her interests and concerns, and the several steps which the king of Babylon should take in pushing on this destruction, <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.1-Ezek.30.19">ver. 1-19</reference>. II. A repetition of a former prophecy against Egypt, just before the desolation of it begun by their own bad conduct, which gradually weakened them and prepared the way for the king of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20-Ezek.30.26">ver. 20-26</reference>. It is all much to the same purport with what we had before.
entries.599e338562a0c4af1b26030af24328f172ab3f74: <div eID="gen18994" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18993" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prophecy against Egypt; Destruction of Egypt Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 572.)</title> <div sID="gen18995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came again unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Howl ye, Woe worth the day! <hi type="super">3</hi> For the day <hi type="italic">is</hi> near, even the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> near, a cloudy day; it shall be the time of the heathen. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the sword shall come upon Egypt, and great pain shall be in Ethiopia, when the slain shall fall in Egypt, and they shall take away her multitude, and her foundations shall be broken down. <hi type="super">5</hi> Ethiopia, and Libya, and Lydia, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; They also that uphold Egypt shall fall; and the pride of her power shall come down: from the tower of Syene shall they fall in it by the sword, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> And they shall be desolate in the midst of the countries <hi type="italic">that are</hi> desolate, and her cities shall be in the midst of the cities <hi type="italic">that are</hi> wasted. <hi type="super">8</hi> And they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when I have set a fire in Egypt, and <hi type="italic">when</hi> all her helpers shall be destroyed. <hi type="super">9</hi> In that day shall messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Ethiopians afraid, and great pain shall come upon them, as in the day of Egypt: for, lo, it cometh. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I will also make the multitude of Egypt to cease by the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon. <hi type="super">11</hi> He and his people with him, the terrible of the nations, shall be brought to destroy the land: and they shall draw their swords against Egypt, and fill the land with the slain. <hi type="super">12</hi> And I will make the rivers dry, and sell the land into the hand of the wicked: and I will make the land waste, and all that is therein, by the hand of strangers: I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause <hi type="italic">their</hi> images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will make Pathros desolate, and will set fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments in No. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt; and I will cut off the multitude of No. <hi type="super">16</hi> And I will set fire in Egypt: Sin shall have great pain, and No shall be rent asunder, and Noph <hi type="italic">shall have</hi> distresses daily. <hi type="super">17</hi> The young men of Aven and of Pi-beseth shall fall by the sword: and these <hi type="italic">cities</hi> shall go into captivity. <hi type="super">18</hi> At Tehaphnehes also the day shall be darkened, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her: as for her, a cloud shall cover her, and her daughters shall go into captivity. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thus will I execute judgments in Egypt: and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18996" type="x-p"/> The prophecy of the destruction of Egypt is here very full and particular, as well as, in the general, very frightful. What can protect a provoking people when the righteous God comes forth to contend with them? <div eID="gen18996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18997" type="x-p"/> I. It shall be a very lamentable destruction, and such as shall occasion great sorrow (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.2-Ezek.30.3">v. 2, 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Howl you;</hi> you may justly shriek now that it is coming, for you will be made to shriek and make hideous outcries when it comes. Cry out, <hi type="italic">Woe worth the day!</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Ah the day! alas because of the day!</hi> the terrible day! <hi type="italic">Woe and alas!</hi> For <hi type="italic">the day is near;</hi> the day we have so long dreaded, so long deserved. It is the <hi type="italic">day of the Lord,</hi> the day in which he will manifest himself as a God of vengeance. You have your day now, when you carry all before you, and trample on all about you, but God will have his day shortly, the day of the revelation of his righteous judgment," <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 13</reference>. It will be <hi type="italic">a cloudy day,</hi> that is, dark and dismal, without the shining forth of any comfort; and it shall threaten a storm—<hi type="italic">fire, and brimstone, and a horrible tempest. It shall be the time of the heathen,</hi> of reckoning with the heathen for all their heathenish practices, that time which David spoke of when God would <hi type="italic">pour out his fury upon the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.6">Ps. lxxix. 6</reference>), when <hi type="italic">they should sink,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.9.15">Ps. ix. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen18997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18998" type="x-p"/> II. It shall be the destruction of Egypt, and of all the states and countries in confederacy with her and in her neighbourhood. 1. Egypt herself shall fall (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.4">v. 4</reference>): The <hi type="italic">sword shall come upon Egypt,</hi> the sword of the Chaldeans, and it shall be a victorious sword, for the <hi type="italic">slain shall fall in Egypt,</hi> fall by it, fall before it. Is the country populous? They shall <hi type="italic">take away her multitude.</hi> Is it strong, and well-fixed? <hi type="italic">Her foundations shall be broken down,</hi> and then the fabric, though built ever so fine, ever so high, will fall of course. 2. Her neighbours and inmates shall fall with her. When the slain fall so thickly in Egypt <hi type="italic">great pain shall be in Ethiopia,</hi> both that in Africa, which is in the neighbourhood of Egypt on one side, and that in Asia, which is near to it on the other side. When their neighbour's house was on fire they could not but apprehend their own in danger; nor were their fears groundless, for they shall all <hi type="italic">fall with them by the sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Ethiopia and Libya</hi> (Cush and Phut, so the Hebrew names are, two of the sons of Ham who are mentioned, and Mizraim, that is, Egypt, between them, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen. x. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">and the Lydians</hi> (who were famous archers, and are spoken of as confederates with Egypt, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer. xlvi. 9</reference>), these shall fall with Egypt and <hi type="italic">Chub</hi> (the Chaldeans, the inhabitants of the inner Libya); these and others were the <hi type="italic">mingled people;</hi> there were those of all these and other countries who upon some account or other resided in Egypt, as did also <hi type="italic">the men of the land that is in league,</hi> some of the remains of the people of Israel and Judah, the <hi type="italic">children of the covenant,</hi> or league, as they are called (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.25">Acts iii. 25</reference>), the <hi type="italic">children of the promise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.28">Gal. iv. 28</reference>. These sojourned in Egypt contrary to God's command, and these shall <hi type="italic">fall with them.</hi> Note, Those that will take their lot with God's enemies shall have their lot with them, yea, though they be in profession the men of the land that is in league with God. <div eID="gen18998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18999" type="x-p"/> III. All that pretend to support the sinking interests of Egypt shall come down under her, shall come down with her (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that uphold Egypt shall fall,</hi> and then Egypt must fall of course. See the justice of God; Egypt pretended to uphold Jerusalem when that was tottering, but proved a deceitful reed; and now those that pretended to uphold Egypt shall prove no better. Those that deceive others are commonly paid in their own coin; they are themselves deceived. 1. Does Egypt think herself upheld by the absolute authority and dominion of her king? The <hi type="italic">pride of her power</hi> shall <hi type="italic">come down,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">v. 6</reference>. The power of the king of Egypt was his pride; but that shall be broken, and humbled. 2. Is the multitude of her people her support? These shall <hi type="italic">fall by the sword,</hi> even <hi type="italic">from the tower of Syene,</hi> which is in the utmost corner of the land, from that side of it by which the enemy shall enter. Both the <hi type="italic">countries</hi> and the <hi type="italic">cities,</hi> the husbandmen and the merchants, shall be desolate, <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.7">v. 7</reference>, as before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.12">ch. xxix. 12</reference>. Even <hi type="italic">the multitude of Egypt shall be made to cease,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.10">v. 10</reference>. That populous country shall be depopulated. The land shall be even <hi type="italic">filled with the slain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.11">v. 11</reference>. 3. Is the river Nile her support, and are the several channels of it a defence to her? "<hi type="italic">I will make the rivers dry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.12">v. 12</reference>), so that those natural fortifications which were thought impregnable, because impassable, shall stand them in no stead." 4. Are her idols a support to her? They shall be destroyed; those imaginary upholders shall appear more than ever to be imaginary, for so images are when they pretend to be deliverers and strongholds (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will cause their images to cease out of Noph.</hi> 5. Is her royal family her support? <hi type="italic">There shall be no more a prince in the land of Egypt;</hi> the royal family shall be extirpated and extinguished, which had continued so long. 6. Is her courage her support, and does she think to uphold herself by the bravery of her men of war, who have now of late been inured to service? That shall fail: <hi type="italic">I will put a fear in the land of Egypt.</hi> 7. Is the rising generation her support? is she upheld by her children, and does she think herself happy because she has her quiver full of them? Alas! <hi type="italic">the young men shall fall by the sword</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.17">v. 17</reference>) and <hi type="italic">the daughters shall go into captivity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.18">v. 18</reference>), and so she shall be robbed of all her hopes. <div eID="gen18999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19000" type="x-p"/> IV. God shall inflict these desolating judgments on Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall know that I am the Lord,</hi> and greater than all gods, than all <hi type="italic">their</hi> gods, when I have <hi type="italic">set a fire in Egypt.</hi> The fire that consumes nations is of God's kindling; and, when he sets fire to a people, <hi type="italic">all their helpers shall be destroyed.</hi> Those that go about to quench the fire shall themselves be devoured by it; for who can stand before him when he is angry? When he <hi type="italic">pours out his fury</hi> upon a place, when he sets fire to it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.15-Ezek.30.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), neither its strength nor its multitude can stand it in any stead. <div eID="gen19000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19001" type="x-p"/> V. The king of Babylon and his army shall be employed as instruments of this destruction: <hi type="italic">The multitude of Egypt shall be made to cease</hi> and be quite cut off <hi type="italic">by the hand of the king of Babylon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.10">v. 10</reference>. Those that undertook to protect Israel from the king of Babylon shall not be able to protect themselves. It is said of the Chaldeans, who should destroy Egypt, 1. That they are <hi type="italic">strangers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.12">v. 12</reference>), who therefore shall show no compassion for old acquaintance-sake, but shall behave strangely towards them. 2. That they are <hi type="italic">the terrible of the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.11">v. 11</reference>), both in respect of force and in respect of fierceness; and, being terrible, they shall make terrible work. (3.) That they are <hi type="italic">the wicked,</hi> who will not be restrained by reason and conscience, the laws of nature or the laws of nations, for they are without law: <hi type="italic">I will sell the land into the hand of the wicked.</hi> They do violence <hi type="italic">unjustly,</hi> as they are wicked; yet, so far as they are instruments in God's hand of executing his judgments, it is on his part justly done. Note, God often makes one wicked man a scourge to another; and even wicked men acquire a title to prey, <hi type="italic">jure belli—by the laws of war,</hi> for God <hi type="italic">sells it into their hands.</hi> <div eID="gen19001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19002" type="x-p"/> VI. No place in the land of Egypt shall be exempted from the fury of the Chaldean army, not the strongest, not the remotest: <hi type="italic">The sword shall go through the land.</hi> Various places are here named: <hi type="italic">Pathros, Zoan, and No</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Sin and Noph</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.15-Ezek.30.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Aven and Pi-beseth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.17">v. 17</reference>), and <hi type="italic">Tehaphnehes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.18">v. 18</reference>. These shall be made desolate, shall be fired, and God's judgments shall be executed upon them, and his fury poured out upon them. Their strength and multitude shall be <hi type="italic">cut off;</hi> they shall have <hi type="italic">great pain,</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">rent asunder</hi> with fear, and shall <hi type="italic">have distresses daily.</hi> Their <hi type="italic">day shall be darkened;</hi> their honours, comforts, and hopes, shall be extinguished. Their <hi type="italic">yokes</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">broken,</hi> so that they shall no more oppress and tyrannize as they have done. The <hi type="italic">pomp of their strength shall cease,</hi> and <hi type="italic">a cloud shall cover them,</hi> a cloud so thick that through it they shall not see any hopes, nor shall their glory <hi type="italic">be seen,</hi> or <hi type="italic">shine further.</hi> And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> the Ethiopians, who are at a distance from them, as well as those who are mingled with them, shall share in their pain and terror. God will by his providence spread the rumour, and the <hi type="italic">careless Ethiopians</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">made afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.9">v. 9</reference>. Note, God can strike a terror upon those that are most secure; fearfulness shall, when he pleases, surprise the most presumptuous hypocrites. <div eID="gen19002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19003" type="x-p"/> The close of this prediction leaves, 1. The land of Egypt mortified: <hi type="italic">Thus will I execute judgments on Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.19">v. 19</reference>. The destruction of Egypt is the <hi type="italic">executing of judgments,</hi> which intimates not only that it is done justly, for its sins, but that it is done regularly and legally, by a judicial sentence. All the executions God does are according to his judgments. 2. The God of Israel herein glorified: <hi type="italic">They shall know that I am the Lord.</hi> The Egyptians shall be made to know it and the people of God shall be made to know it better. <hi type="italic">The Lord is known by the judgments which he executes.</hi>
entries.082c77f2a6e23a9a6f13f1c8c13f50379c506f93: <div eID="gen19003" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Destruction of Egypt Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 572.)</title> <div sID="gen19004" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first <hi type="italic">month,</hi> in the seventh <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">21</hi> Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed, to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword. <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms, the strong, and that which was broken; and I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand. <hi type="super">23</hi> And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries. <hi type="super">24</hi> And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and put my sword in his hand: but I will break Pharaoh's arms, and he shall groan before him with the groanings of a deadly wounded <hi type="italic">man.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> But I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharaoh shall fall down; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when I shall put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall stretch it out upon the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">26</hi> And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them among the countries; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen19004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19005" type="x-p"/> This short prophecy of the weakening of the power of Egypt was delivered about the time that the army of the Egyptians, which attempted to raise the siege of Jerusalem, was frustrated in its enterprises, and returned <hi type="italic">re infectâ—without accomplishing their purpose;</hi> whereupon the king of Babylon renewed the siege and carried his point. The kingdom of Egypt was very ancient, and had been for many ages considerable. That of Babylon had but lately arrived at its great pomp and power, being built upon the ruins of the kingdom of Assyria. Now it is with them as it is with families and states, some are growing up, others are declining and going back; one must increase and the others must of course decrease. <div eID="gen19005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19006" type="x-p"/> I. It is here foretold that the king of Egypt shall grow weaker and weaker. The extent of his territories shall be abridged, his wealth and power shall be diminished, and he shall become less able than ever to help either himself or his friend. 1. This was in part done already (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have broken the arm of Pharaoh,</hi> some time ago. One arm of that kingdom might well be reckoned broken when the king of Babylon routed the forces of Pharaoh-Necho at Carchemish (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer. xlvi. 2</reference>), and made himself master of <hi type="italic">all that pertained to Egypt from the river of Egypt to Euphrates,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2 Kings xxiv. 7</reference>. Egypt had been long in gathering strength and extending its dominions, and therefore, that there may be a proportion observed in providence, it loses its strength slowly and by degrees. It was soon after the king of Egypt slew good king Josiah, and in the same reign, that its arm was thus broken, and it received that fatal blow which it never recovered. Before Egypt's heart and neck were broken its arm was. God's judgments come upon a people by steps, that they may meet him repenting. When the arm of Egypt is broken <hi type="italic">it shall not be bound up to be healed,</hi> for none can heal the wounds that God gives but he himself. Those whom he disarms, whom he disables, cannot again hold the sword. 2. This was to be done again. One arm was broken before, and something was done towards the setting of it, towards the healing of the deadly wound that was given to the beast. But now (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am against Pharaoh, and will break both his arms,</hi> both <hi type="italic">the strong</hi> and that <hi type="italic">which was broken</hi> and set again. Note, If less judgments do not prevail to humble and reform sinners, God will send greater. Now God will <hi type="italic">cause the sword to fall out of his hand,</hi> which he caught hold of as thinking himself strong enough to hold it. It is repeated (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will break Pharaoh's arms.</hi> He had been a cruel oppressor to the people of God formerly, and of late the <hi type="italic">staff of a broken rod</hi> to them; and now God by breaking his arms reckons with him for both. God justly breaks that power which is abused either to put wrongs upon people or to put cheats upon them. But this is not all; (1.) The king of Egypt shall be dispirited when he finds himself in danger of the king of Babylon's forces: he <hi type="italic">shall groan before him with the groaning of a deadly wounded man.</hi> Note, It is common for those that are most elated in their prosperity to be most dejected and disheartened in their adversity. Pharaoh, even before the sword touches him, shall groan as if he had received his death's wound. (2.) The people of Egypt shall be dispersed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.23">v. 23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.26">again v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will scatter them among the nations.</hi> Other nations had mingled with them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">v. 5</reference>); now they shall be mingled with other nations, and seek shelter in them, and so be made to know that the Lord is righteous. <div eID="gen19006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19007" type="x-p"/> II. It is here foretold that the king of Babylon shall grow stronger and stronger, <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.24-Ezek.30.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">Put strength</hi> into the king of Babylon's arms, that he may be able to go through the service he is designed for. 2. That he will <hi type="italic">put a sword,</hi> his sword, into the king of Babylon's hand, which signified his giving him a commission and furnishing him with arms for carrying on a war, particularly against Egypt. Note, As judges on the bench, like Pilate (<reference osisRef="John.19.11">John xix. 11</reference>), so generals in the field, like Nebuchadnezzar, have no power but what is given them from above.  <chapter eID="Ezek.30"/> <div eID="gen19007" type="x-p"/>

entries.d71ed2ba13f2372047b44d5904c79f44bdd7b471: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11591"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 30</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.30.1-Ezek.30.26">Eze 30:1-26</reference>. Continuation of the Prophecies against Egypt.</title> <div sID="gen21004" type="x-p"/> Two distinct messages: (1) At <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.1-Ezek.30.19">Eze 30:1-19</reference>, a repetition of <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1-Ezek.29.16">Eze 29:1-16</reference>, with fuller details of lifelike distinctness. The date is probably not long after that mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17">Eze 29:17</reference>, on the eve of Nebuchadnezzar's march against Egypt after subjugating Tyre. (2) A vision relating directly to Pharaoh and the overthrow of his kingdom; communicated at an earlier date, the seventh of the first month of the eleventh year. Not a year after the date in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1">Eze 29:1</reference>, and three months before the taking of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen21004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11591"/><hi type="bold">2. Woe worth the day!--</hi>that is, Alas for the day! <div eID="gen21005" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ad528793a05bf83f2bb8fd048a4115f09b276a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11592"/><div sID="gen21006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11592"/><hi type="bold">3. the time of the heathen--</hi>namely, for taking vengeance on them. The judgment on Egypt is the beginning of a world-wide judgment on all the heathen enemies of God (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.15">Joe 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2:1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.21">3:1-21</reference>; Ob 15). <div eID="gen21006" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f5c83d0785cb3ddaeebe74d78273da493a9f019: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11593"/><div sID="gen21007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11593"/><hi type="bold">4. pain--</hi>literally, "pangs with trembling as of a woman in childbirth." <div eID="gen21007" type="x-p"/>
entries.da0f1957a918c0a70999ba685c9b5770af4624a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11594"/><div sID="gen21008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11594"/><hi type="bold">5. the mingled people--</hi>the mercenary troops of Egypt from various lands, mostly from the interior of Africa (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10">Eze 27:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.20">Jr 25:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">46:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen21008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chub--</hi>the people named Kufa on the monuments [Havernick], a people considerably north of Palestine [Wilkinson]; Coba or Chobat, a city of Mauritania [Maurer].<div eID="gen21009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men of the land that is in league--</hi>too definite an expression to mean merely, "men in league" with Egypt; rather, "sons of the land of the covenant," that is, the Jews who migrated to Egypt and carried Jeremiah with them (Jr 42:1-44:30). Even they shall not escape (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.22">Jr 42:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.14">44:14</reference>). <div eID="gen21010" type="x-p"/>
entries.42bf760394bda5aa733f7470571516d0ab4529a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11595"/><div sID="gen21011" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11595"/><hi type="bold">6. from the tower of Syene--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">Eze 29:10</reference>). <div eID="gen21011" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c2bbfad1c169007d5753bd7dc66b07e874ab98c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11596"/><div sID="gen21012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11596"/><hi type="bold">7. in the midst of ... countries ... desolate--</hi>Egypt shall fare no better than they (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">Eze 29:10</reference>). <div eID="gen21012" type="x-p"/>
entries.f310b48da77f0b29007955f9c9a0638a448c8648: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11597"/><div sID="gen21013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11597"/><hi type="bold">9. messengers ... in ships to ... Ethiopians--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Is 18:1</reference>, 2). The cataracts interposing between them and Egypt should not save them. Egyptians "fleeing from before Me" in My execution of judgment, as "messengers" in "skiffs" ("vessels of bulrushes," <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Is 18:2</reference>) shall go up the Nile as far as navigable, to announce the advance of the Chaldeans.<div eID="gen21013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as in the day of Egypt--</hi>The day of Ethiopia's "pain" shall come shortly, as Egypt's day came. <div eID="gen21014" type="x-p"/>
entries.d69f9ba26b7d2498d7ff654b90aafa6b46e853a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11598"/><div sID="gen21015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11598"/><hi type="bold">10. the multitude--</hi>the large population. <div eID="gen21015" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f7e58eb7769f393a97ad3edee57957fd2eede2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11599"/><div sID="gen21016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11599"/><hi type="bold">12. rivers--</hi>the artificial canals made from the Nile for irrigation. The drying up of these would cause scarcity of grain, and so prepare the way for the invaders (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5-Isa.19.10">Is 19:5-10</reference>). <div eID="gen21016" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd017aec5c095931748305ffcf3f72a0e89d8f1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11600"/><div sID="gen21017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11600"/><hi type="bold">13. Noph--</hi>Memphis, the capital of Middle Egypt, and the stronghold of "idols." Though no record exists of Nebuchadnezzar's "destroying" these, we know from Herodotus and others, that Cambyses took Pelusium, the key of Egypt, by placing before his army dogs, cats, &c., all held sacred in Egypt, so that no Egyptian would use any weapon against them. He slew Apis, the sacred ox, and burnt other idols of Egypt.<div eID="gen21017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no more a prince--</hi>referring to the anarchy that prevailed in the civil wars between Apries and Amasis at the time of Nebuchadnezzar's invasion. There shall no more be a prince of the land of Egypt, ruling the whole country; or, no independent prince. <div eID="gen21018" type="x-p"/>
entries.953ffaaee0ee826e7359551326d505ee8368fdeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11601"/><div sID="gen21019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11601"/><hi type="bold">14. Pathros--</hi>Upper Egypt, with "No" or Thebes its capital (famed for its stupendous buildings, of which grand ruins remain), in antithesis to Zoan or Tanis, a chief city in Lower Egypt, within the Delta. <div eID="gen21019" type="x-p"/>
entries.b011738da117637e0f9fc358513595ab5ac3e47a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11602"/><div sID="gen21020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11602"/><hi type="bold">15. Sin--</hi>that is, Pelusium, the frontier fortress on the northeast, therefore called "the strength (that is, the key) of Egypt." It stands in antithesis to No or Thebes at the opposite end of Egypt; that is, I will afflict Egypt from one end to the other. <div eID="gen21020" type="x-p"/>
entries.eebaa9afcead14322732a94eea68cca5b0043bb9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11603"/><div sID="gen21021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11603"/><hi type="bold">16. distresses daily--</hi>Maurer translates, "enemies during the day," that is, open enemies who do not wait for the covert of night to make their attacks (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.6.4">Jr 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">15:8</reference>). However, the Hebrew, though rarely, is sometimes rendered (see <reference osisRef="Ps.13.2">Psa 13:2</reference>) as in English Version. <div eID="gen21021" type="x-p"/>
entries.86dffc6e8003131fb906366b57073fa860600039: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11604"/><div sID="gen21022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11604"/><hi type="bold">17. Aven--</hi>meaning "vanity" or "iniquity": applied, by a slight change of the Hebrew name, to On or Heliopolis, in allusion to its idolatry. Here stood the temple of the sun, whence it was called in Hebrew, Beth-shemesh (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.13">Jr 43:13</reference>). The Egyptian hieroglyphics call it, Re Athom, the sun, the father of the gods, being impersonate in Athom or Adam, the father of mankind.<div eID="gen21022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pi-beseth--</hi>that is, Bubastis, in Lower Egypt, near the Pelusiac branch of the Nile: notorious for the worship of the goddess of the same name (Coptic, Pasht), the granite stones of whose temple still attest its former magnificence.<div eID="gen21023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these cities--</hi>rather, as the Septuagint, "the women," namely, of Aven and Pi-beseth, in antithesis to "the young men." So in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.18">Eze 30:18</reference>, "daughters shall go into captivity" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen21024" type="x-p"/>
entries.69742e4ee893622a95330ecf7c1f7251d625f808: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11605"/><div sID="gen21025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11605"/><hi type="bold">18. Tehaphnehes--</hi>called from the queen of Egypt mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.19">1Ki 11:19</reference>. The same as Daphne, near Pelusium, a royal residence of the Pharaohs (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.7">Jr 43:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.43.9">9</reference>). Called Hanes (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.4">Is 30:4</reference>).<div eID="gen21025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">break ... the yokes of Egypt--</hi>that is, the tyrannical supremacy which she exercised over other nations. Compare "bands of their yoke" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.7">Eze 34:7</reference>).<div eID="gen21026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a cloud--</hi>namely, of calamity. <div eID="gen21027" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fd230e4e18f14124962a7ccb40cb599af8cb741: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11606"/><div sID="gen21028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11606"/>20. Here begins the earlier vision, not long after that in the twenty-ninth chapter, about three months before the taking of Jerusalem, as to Pharaoh and his kingdom. <div eID="gen21028" type="x-p"/>
entries.08d4f054d592ac863cbdfddd54fcd604fae3f9f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11607"/><div sID="gen21029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11607"/><hi type="bold">21. broken ... arm of Pharaoh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.37.17">Psa 37:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.25">Jr 48:25</reference>). Referring to the defeat which Pharaoh-hophra sustained from the Chaldeans, when trying to raise the siege of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7">7</reference>); and previous to the deprivation of Pharaoh-necho of all his conquests from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>); also to the Egyptian disaster in Cyrene. <div eID="gen21029" type="x-p"/>
entries.519292e059ad94b1a843a4abf78e2d1be4ef2302: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11608"/><div sID="gen21030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11608"/><hi type="bold">22. arms--</hi>Not only the "one arm" broken already (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">Eze 30:21</reference>) was not to be healed, but the other two should be broken. Not a corporal wound, but a breaking of the power of Pharaoh is intended.<div eID="gen21030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cause ... sword to fall out of ... hand--</hi>deprive him of the resources of making war. <chapter eID="Ezek.30"/>

entries.c23636c056534946688e3280a85c93796107c7b4: <div eID="gen32154" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32155" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32156" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32156" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32155" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32157" type="x-p"/> This chapter describes, with great force and elegance, the ruin of Egypt and all her allies by the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Eze.30.1-Eze.30.11">Eze 30:1-11</reference>; with an amplification of the distress of the principal cities of Egypt on that occasion, <reference osisRef="Eze.30.12-Eze.30.19">Eze 30:12-19</reference>. The remaining verses are a short prophecy relating to the same event, and therefore annexed to the longer one preceding, although this was predicted sooner, <reference osisRef="Eze.30.20-Eze.30.26">Eze 30:20-26</reference>.
entries.244082b0f306ed4226f01e3e33c54b62b37baab6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32158" type="x-p"/> Howl ye, Wo worth the day! - My Old MS. Bible, - Soule gee, woo woo to the day! הילילו הה ליום heylilu, hah laiyom! "Howl ye, Alas for the day!" The reading in our present text is taken from Coverdale's Bible, 1536. The expressions signify that a most dreadful calamity was about to fall on Egypt and the neighboring countries, called here the "time of the heathen," or of the nations; the day of calamity to them. They are afterwards specified, Ethiopia, Libya, Lydia, and Chub, and the mingled people, probably persons from different nations, who had followed the ill fortune of Pharaoh-hophra or Pharaoh-apries, when he fled from Amasis, and settled in Upper Egypt.
entries.7a26adc5a2887086557ab147d61bbd4d041770ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32159" type="x-p"/> Lydia - This place is not well known. The Ludim were contiguous to Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.13">Gen 11:13</reference>. <div eID="gen32159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32160" type="x-p"/> Chub - The Cubians, placed by Ptolemy in the Mareotis. But probably instead of וכוב vechub, "and Chub," we should read וכל vechol, "and All the men of the land," etc. The Septuagint adds "the Persians and the Cretans."
entries.3d68f9e02a4c14c72a91e3d8ec0992650701b377: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32161" type="x-p"/> Shall be desolate - All these countries shall be desolated, and the places named shall be chief in these desolations.
entries.c8c71076fe3da1366839581dad6ef6883a65c3b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32162" type="x-p"/> Messengers go forth from me in ships - Ships can ascend the Nile up to Syene or Essuan, by the cataracts; and when Nebuchadnezzar's vessels went up, they struck terror into the Ethiopians. They are represented here as the "messengers of God."
entries.b77956e5277d6018cd957e34245ad1eb697c9d9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen32162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32163" type="x-p"/> I will make the rivers dry - As the overflowing of the Nile was the grand cause of fertility to Egypt, the drying it up, or preventing that annual inundation, must be the cause of dearth, famine, etc. By rivers, we may understand the various canals cut from the Nile to carry water into the different parts of the land. When the Nile did not rise to its usual height these canals were quite dry.
entries.f857ad5e038276f7f27611eafbf075d79164d325: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32164" type="x-p"/> Their images to cease out of Noph - Afterwards Memphis, and now Cairo or Kahira. This was the seat of Egyptian idolatry; the place where Apis was particularly worshipped. <div eID="gen32164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32165" type="x-p"/> No more a prince of the land of Egypt - Not one, from that time to the present day. See the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.29.14">Eze 29:14</reference>.
entries.bc7564bc63fb6f39a0f39c6c2328058d45dddf34: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32166" type="x-p"/> I will make Pathros desolate - See <reference osisRef="Eze.29.14">Eze 29:14</reference>. <div eID="gen32166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32167" type="x-p"/> Zoan - Tanis, the ancient capital of Egypt. <div eID="gen32167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32168" type="x-p"/> No - Diospolis, or Thebes, the city of Jupiter.
entries.f73c7dde41c54a6b6d87f33febb22663514dc733: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32169" type="x-p"/> My fury upon Sin - Pelusium, a strong city of Egypt, on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea.
entries.3a89455ac089833fbe20bad35d02ee0841f4d6f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32170" type="x-p"/> Noph - Cairo or Kahira; see <reference osisRef="Eze.30.13">Eze 30:13</reference>.
entries.b7efb1a0f21176247bd39456a5a657b47f5e9277: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32171" type="x-p"/> Aven - Or On, the famous Heliopolis, or city of the sun. <div eID="gen32171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32172" type="x-p"/> Pibeseth - Bubastum or Bubaste, by a slight alteration of the letters. It is situated on the eastern branch of the Nile, towards Arabia.
entries.765811f1c82a493267967b4fbaf777d6e984c2dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32173" type="x-p"/> Tehaphnehes - Called also Tahapanes, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.16">Jer 2:16</reference>. This is the Pelusian Daphne. <div eID="gen32173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32174" type="x-p"/> Break there the yokes - The sceptres. Nebuchadnezzar broke the scepter of Egypt when he confirmed the kingdom to Amasis, who had rebelled against Apries.
entries.cc210cb7dba0ab64a7dcc15db119445e1c28bde6: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32175" type="x-p"/> In the eleventh year, in the first month, in the seventh day - This was the eleventh year of the captivity of Jeconiah, and the date here answers to April 26, A.M. 3416; a prophecy anterior by several years to that already delivered. In collecting the writings of Ezekiel, more care was taken to put all that related to one subject together, than to attend to chronological arrangement.
entries.1b74ed9ada1b40c4304659a98c709a48dabb53d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32176" type="x-p"/> I have broken the arm of Pharaoh - Perhaps this may refer to his defeat by Nebuchadnezzar, when he was coming with the Egyptian army to succor Jerusalem.
entries.5890f44113f08d11e22b77554b4d58e733ce9ae8: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen32176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32177" type="x-p"/> I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand - When the arm is broken, the sword will naturally fall. But these expressions show that the Egyptians would be rendered wholly useless to Zedekiah, and should never more recover their political strength. This was the case from the time of the rebellion of Amasis.
entries.2a2270495331616c464954339ec06d0313186423: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen32177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32178" type="x-p"/> I will scatter the Egyptians - Several fled with Apries to Upper Egypt; and when Nebuchadnezzar wasted the country, he carried many of them to Babylon. See on <reference osisRef="Eze.29.12">Eze 29:12</reference> (note).  <chapter eID="Ezek.30"/> <div eID="gen32178" type="x-p"/>

entries.23dfb6a2da89f49920d7ab16a2a5997acf14ab81: <div eID="gen15085" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Day of Judgment upon Egypt - Ezekiel 30:1-19</title> <div sID="gen15086" type="x-p"/> Commencing with a call to lamentation, the prophet announces that the Lord’s day of judgment upon the nations is near at hand, and will burst upon Egypt, and the nations in alliance with it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.2-Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:2-5</reference>). He then depicts in three strophes, with the introductory words 'כּה אמר , the execution for this judgment, namely: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) the destruction of the might of Egypt and the devastation of the land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6-Ezek.30.9">Eze 30:6-9</reference>); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) the enemy by whom the judgment will be accomplished (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.10-Ezek.30.12">Eze 30:10-12</reference>); and (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) the extermination of the idols of Egypt, the conquest and demolition of its fortresses, the slaughter of its male population, and the captivity of the daughters of the land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13-Ezek.30.19">Eze 30:13-19</reference>). <div eID="gen15086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15087" type="x-p"/> The heading does not contain any chronological information; and the contents furnish no definite <hi type="italic">criteria</hi> for determining with precision the date of the prophecy. Jerome assigns this oracle to the same period as the prophecy in Ezekiel 29:1-16, whilst others connect it more closely with <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:17-21</reference>, and regard it as the latest of all Ezekiel’s prophecies. The latter is the conclusion adopted by Rosenmüller, Hävernick, Hitzig, Kliefoth, and some others. The principal argument adduced for linking it on to Eze 29:17. is, that in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.3">Eze 30:3</reference> the day of judgment upon Egypt is threatened as near at hand, and this did not apply to the tenth year (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1">Eze 29:1</reference>), though it was perfectly applicable to the twenty-seventh (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17">Eze 29:17</reference>), when the siege of Tyre was ended, and Nebuchadnezzar was on the point of attacking Egypt. But the expression, “the day of the Lord is near at hand,” is so relative a chronological phrase, that nothing definite can be gathered from it as to the date at which an oracle was composed. Nor does the fact that our prophecy stands after the prophecy in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:17-21</reference>, which is furnished with a date, prove anything; for the other prophecies which follow, and are furnished with dates, all belong to a much earlier period. It is very evident from this that <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:17-21</reference> is inserted without regard to chronological sequence, and consequently Ezekiel 30:1-19 may just as well belong to the period between the tenth month of the tenth year (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1">Eze 29:1</reference>) and the first month of the eleventh year (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20">Eze 30:20</reference>), as to the twenty-seventh year (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17">Eze 29:17</reference>), since all the reasons assigned for the closer connection of our prophecy with the one immediately preceding (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.21">Eze 29:17-21</reference>), which is supposed to indicate similarity of date, are invalid; whilst, on the other hand, the resemblance of <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">Eze 30:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.17">Eze 30:17</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">Eze 29:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.12">Eze 29:12</reference> is not sufficient to warrant the assumption of a contemporaneous origin. <div eID="gen15087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15088" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.1-Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen15088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15089" type="x-p"/> Announcement of the judgment upon Egypt and its allies. - Eze 30:1. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 30:2. <hi type="italic">Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Howl ye! Woe to the day!</hi> Eze 30:3. <hi type="italic">For the day is near, the day of Jehovah near, a day of cloud, the time of the heathen will it be.</hi> Eze 30:4. <hi type="italic">And the sword will come upon Egypt, and there will be pangs in Ethiopia, when the slain fall in Egypt, and they take her possessions, and her foundations are destroyed.</hi> Eze 30:5. <hi type="italic">Ethiopians and Libyans and Lydians, and all the rabble, and Chub, and the sons of the covenant land, will fall by the sword with them.</hi> - In the announcement of the judgment in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.30.2">Eze 30:2</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.3">Eze 30:3</reference>, Ezekiel rests upon <reference osisRef="Joel.1.13">Joe 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.15">Joe 1:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>, where the designation already applied to the judgment upon the heathen world by Obadiah, viz., “the day of Jehovah” (Oba 1:15), is followed by such a picture of the nearness and terrible nature of that day, that even Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.6">Isa 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.9">Isa 13:9</reference>) and Zephaniah (Zep 1:7, Zep 1:14) appropriate the words of Joel. Ezekiel also does the same, with this exception, that he uses ההּ instead of אההּ, and adds to the force of the expression by the repetition of קרוב יום. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.30.3">Eze 30:3</reference></hi>, the words from יום ענן to יהיה are not to be taken together as forming one sentence, “a day of cloud will the time of the nations be” (De Wette), because the idea of a “time of the nations” has not been mentioned before, so as to prepare the way for a description of its real nature here. יום ענן and עת גּוים contain two co-ordinate affirmations concerning the day of Jehovah. It will be a day of cloud, i.e., of great calamity (as in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>), and a time of the heathen, i.e., when heathen (גּוים without the article) are judged, when their might is to be shattered (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Isa 13:22</reference>). This day is coming upon Egypt, which is to succumb to the sword. Ethiopia will be so terrified at this, that it will writhe convulsively with anguish (חלחלה, as in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.11">Nah 2:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.21.3">Isa 21:3</reference>). לקח המנהּ signifies the plundering and removal of the possessions of the land, like נשׂא המנהּ in Eze 29:19. The subject to לקחוּ is indefinite, “they,” i.e., the enemy. The foundations of Egypt, which are to be destroyed, are not the foundations of its buildings, but may be understood in a figurative sense as relating to persons, after the analogy of <reference osisRef="Isa.19.10">Isa 19:10</reference>; but the notion that Cush, Phut, etc. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.9">Eze 30:9</reference>), i.e., the mercenary troops obtained from those places, which are called the props of Egypt in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">Eze 30:6</reference>, are intended, as Hitzig assumes, is not only extremely improbable, but decidedly erroneous. The announcement in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">Eze 30:6</reference>, that Cush, Phut, etc., are to fall by the sword along with the Egyptians (אתּם), is sufficient of itself to show that these tribes, even if they were auxiliaries or mercenaries of Egypt, did not constitute the foundations of the Egyptian state and kingdom; but that, on the contrary, Egypt possessed a military force composed of native troops, which was simply strengthened by auxiliaries and allies. We there interpret יסדותיה, after the analogy of <reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference>, as referring to the real foundations of the state, the regulations and institutions on which the stability and prosperity of the kingdom rest. <div eID="gen15089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15090" type="x-p"/> The neighbouring, friendly, and allied peoples will also be smitten by the judgment together with the Egyptians. <hi type="italic">Cush</hi>, i.e., the Ethiopians, <hi type="italic">Phut</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lud</hi>, i.e., the Libyans and African Lydians (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10">Eze 27:10</reference>), are mentioned here primarily as auxiliaries of Egypt, because, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference>, they served in Necho’s army. By כּל־הערב, the whole of the mixed crowd (see the comm. on 1Ki 10:15 - πάντες οἱ ἐπίμικτοι, lxx), we are then to understand the mercenary soldiers in the Egyptian army, which were obtained from different nations (chiefly Greeks, Ionians, and Carians, οἱ επίκουροι, as they are called by Herodotus, iii. 4, etc.). In addition to these, כּוּב ,eseht  (ἁπ λεγ.) is also mentioned. Hävernick connects this name with the people of <hi type="italic">Kufa</hi>, so frequently met with on the Egyptian monuments. But, according to Wilkinson (<hi type="italic">Manners</hi>, etc., I 1, pp. 361ff.), they inhabited a portion of Asia farther north even than Palestine; and he ranks them (p. 379) among the enemies of Egypt. Hitzig therefore imagines that <hi type="italic">Kufa</hi> is probably to be found in <hi type="italic">Kohistan</hi>, a district of Media, from which, however, the Egyptians can hardly have obtained mercenary troops. And so long as nothing certain can be gathered from the advancing Egyptological researches with regard to the name <hi type="italic">Cub</hi>, the conjecture that כּוּב is a mis-spelling for לוּב is not to be absolutely set aside, the more especially as this conjecture is naturally suggested by the לוּבים of <reference osisRef="Nah.3.9">Nah 3:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.8">2Ch 16:8</reference>, and the form לוּב by the side of לוּבים is analogous to לוּד by the side of לוּדים in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference>, whilst the <hi type="italic">Liby-Aegyptii</hi> of the ancients, who are to be understood by the term לוּבים (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Gen 10:13</reference>), would be quite in keeping here. On the other hand, the conjecture offered by Gesenius (<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 664), viz., נוּב, <hi type="italic">Nubia</hi>, has but a very weak support in the Arabic translator; and the supposition that לוּב may have been the earlier Hebrew form for Nubia (Hitzig), is destitute of any solid foundation. Maurer suggests <hi type="italic">Cob</hi>, a city (<hi type="italic">municipium</hi>) of Mauretania, in the <hi type="italic">Itiner. Anton.</hi> p. 17, ed. Wessel. - The following expression, “sons of the covenant land,” is also obscure. Hitzig has correctly observed, that it cannot be synonymous with בּעלי , their allies. But we certainly cannot admit that the covenant land (made definite by the article) is Canaan, the Holy Land (Hitzig and Kliefoth); although Jerome writes without reserve, <hi type="italic">de filiis terrae foederis</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">de populo Judaeorum</hi>; and the lxx in their translation, καὶ τῶν υιῶν τῆς διαθήκης μου, undoubtedly thought of the Jews, who fled to Egypt, according to Theodoret’s exposition, along with Jeremiah after the destruction of Jerusalem and the murder of the governor Gedaliah, for fear of the vengeance of the Chaldeans (Jer 42-43, and 44). For the application of the expression “land of the covenant” to the Holy Land is never met with either in the Old or New Testament, and cannot be inferred, as Hitzig supposes, from <reference osisRef="Ps.74.20">Psa 74:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.11.28">Dan 11:28</reference>, or supported in any way from either the epithet “the land of promise” in <reference osisRef="Heb.11.9">Heb 11:9</reference>, or from <reference osisRef="Acts.3.25">Act 3:25</reference>, where Peter calls the Jews “the children of the prophets and of the covenant.” We therefore agree with Schmieder in regarding ארץ as signifying a definite region, though one unknown to us, in the vicinity of Egypt, which was inhabited by a tribe that was independent of the Egyptians, yet bound to render help in time of war.
entries.b52d9e2edc5773cd48b7067fcb3ea988caae7003: <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6-Ezek.30.9">Eze 30:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen15090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15091" type="x-p"/> All the supports and helpers of Egypt will fall, and the whole land with its cities will be laid waste. - Eze 30:6. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Those who support Egypt will fall, and its proud might will sink; from Migdol to Syene will they fall by the sword therein, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> Eze 30:7. <hi type="italic">And they will lie waste in the midst of waste lands, and its cities be in the midst of desolate cities.</hi> Eze 30:8. <hi type="italic">They shall learn that I am Jehovah, when I bring fire into Egypt, and all its helpers are shattered.</hi> Eze 30:9. <hi type="italic">In that day will messengers go forth from me in ships to terrify the confident Ethiopia, and there will be writing among them as in the day of Egypt; for, behold, it cometh.</hi> - ”Those who support Egypt” are not the auxiliary tribes and allies, for they are included in the term עזריה in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.8">Eze 30:8</reference>, but the idols and princes (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13">Eze 30:13</reference>), the fortified cities (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.15">Eze 30:15</reference>), and the warriors (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.17">Eze 30:17</reference>), who formed the foundation of the might of the kingdom. גּאון , “the pride of its might,” which is an expression applied in <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference> to the temple at Jerusalem, is to be taken here in a general sense, and understood not merely of the temples and idols of Egypt, but as the sum total of all the things on which the Egyptians rested the might of their kingdom, and on the ground of which they regarded it as indestructible. For 'ממּגדּל וגו, see the comm. on Eze 29:10. The subject to יפּלוּ בהּ is the 'סמכי מצר. <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.7">Eze 30:7</reference> is almost a literal repetition of <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.12">Eze 29:12</reference>; and the subject to נשׁמּוּ is מצרים regarded as a country, though the number and gender of the verb have both been regulated by the form of the noun. The fire which God will bring into Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.8">Eze 30:8</reference>) is the fire of war. Eze 30:9. The tidings of this judgment of God will be carried by messengers to Ethiopia, and there awaken the most terrible dread of a similar fate. In the first hemistich, the prophet has <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference> floating before his mind. The messengers, who carry the tidings thither, are not the warlike forces of Chaldea, who are sent thither by God; for they would not be content with performing the service of messengers alone. We have rather to think of Egyptians, who flee by ship to Ethiopia. The messengers go, מלפני, from before Jehovah, who is regarded as being present in Egypt, while executing judgment there (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Isa 19:1</reference>). צים, as in Num 24:24 = ציּים (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">Dan 11:30</reference>), ships, <hi type="italic">trieres</hi>, according to the Rabbins, in Hieron. <hi type="italic">Symm</hi>. on <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Isa 33:21</reference>, and the Targum on Num. (cf. Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 1156). בּטח is attached to כּוּשׁ, Cush secure or confident, equivalent to the confident Cush (Ewald, §287 <hi type="italic">c</hi>). 'והיתה חלח, repeated from Eze 30:4. בּהם, among the Ethiopians. 'כּיום מצר, as in the day of Egypt, i.e., not the present day of Egypt’s punishment, for the Ethiopians have only just heard of this from the messengers; but the ancient, well-known day of judgment upon Egypt (Exo 15:12.). Ewald and Hitzig follow the lxx in taking כּיום for בּיום; but this is both incorrect and unsuitable, and reduces 'בּיום מצר into a tame repetition of בּיּום החוּא. The subject to הנּה באה is to be taken from the context, viz., that which is predicted in the preceding verses (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6-Ezek.30.8">Eze 30:6-8</reference>).
entries.9a3826d99e56a9826eb8c38dd0e4f604535e89f6: <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.10-Ezek.30.12">Eze 30:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen15091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15092" type="x-p"/> The executors of the judgment. - Eze 30:10. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, And I will put an end to the tumult of Egypt through Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.</hi> Eze 30:11. <hi type="italic">He and his people with him, violent of the nations, will be brought to destroy the land; they will draw their swords against Egypt, and fill the land with slain.</hi> Eze 30:12. <hi type="italic">And I will make the rivers dry, and sell the land into the hand of wicked men, and lay waste the land and its fulness by the hand of foreigners; I Jehovah have spoken it.</hi> - המון cannot be understood as signifying either the multitude of people only, or the abundance of possessions alone; for השׁבּית is not really applicable to either of these meanings. They are evidently both included in the המון, which signifies the tumult of the people in the possession and enjoyment of their property (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.13">Eze 26:13</reference>). The expression is thus specifically explained in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.11">Eze 30:11</reference> and Eze 30:12. Nebuchadnezzar will destroy the land with his men of war, slaying the people with its possessions. עריצי, as in Eze 28:7. מוּבאים, as in Eze 23:42. 'הריק וגו, cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.14">Eze 12:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.28">Eze 12:28</reference>; 7. חלל...מלאוּ, as in Eze 11:6. יארים, the arms and canals of the Nile, by which the land was watered, and on which the fertility and prosperity of Egypt depended. The drying up of the arms of the Nile must not be restricted, therefore, to the fact that God would clear away the hindrances to the entrance of the Chaldeans into the land, but embraces also the removal of the natural resources on which the country depended. מכר, to sell a land or people into the hand of any one, i.e., to deliver it into his power (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference>; Jdg 2:14, etc.). For the fact itself, see <reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">Isa 19:4</reference>-6. For 'השׁמּתי וגו, see Eze 19:7.
entries.ccd543872588cce1820e55ef5c01fa40d015c1bd: <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13-Ezek.30.19">Eze 30:13-19</reference> <div eID="gen15092" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Further Description of the Judgment</title> <div sID="gen15093" type="x-p"/> Eze 30:13. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, I will exterminate the idols and cut off the deities from Noph, and there shall be no more a prince from the land of Egypt; and I put terror upon the land of Egypt.</hi> Eze 30:14. <hi type="italic">And I lay Pathros waste, and bring fire into Zoan, and execute judgments upon No;</hi> Eze 30:15. <hi type="italic">And I pour out my fury upon Sin, the stronghold of Egypt, and cut off the multitude of No;</hi> Eze 30:16. <hi type="italic">And I put fire in Egypt; Sin will writhe in pain, and No will be broken open, and Noph - enemies by day.</hi> Eze 30:17. <hi type="italic">The men of On and Bubastus will fall by the sword, and they themselves will go into captivity.</hi> Eze 30:18. <hi type="italic">At Tachpanches the day will be darkened when I shatter the yokes of Egypt there, and an end will be put to its proud haughtiness; cloud will cover it, and its daughters till go into captivity.</hi> Eze 30:19. <hi type="italic">And thus I execute judgments upon Egypt, that they may know that I am Jehovah.</hi> - Egypt will lose its idols and its princes (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.46.25">Jer 46:25</reference>). גּלּוּלים and אלילים are synonymous, signifying not the images, but the deities; the former being the ordinary epithet applied to false deities by Ezekiel (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.4">Eze 6:4</reference>), the latter traceable to the reading of Isa 19:1. נף, contracted from מנף, <hi type="italic">Manoph</hi> or <hi type="italic">Menoph</hi> = מף in Hos 9:6, is <hi type="italic">Memphis</hi>, the ancient capital of Lower Egypt, with the celebrated temple of <hi type="italic">Ptah</hi>, one of the principal seats of Egyptian idolatry (see the comm. on Hos 9:6 and <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Isa 19:13</reference>). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13">Eze 30:13</reference></hi> מארץ מצר' belongs to נשׂיא, there shall be no more a prince from the land of Egypt, i.e., a native prince. נתן יראה, to put fear upon (cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.26.17">Eze 26:17</reference></hi>). From Lower Egypt Ezekiel passes in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.14">Eze 30:14</reference> to Upper Egypt (<hi type="italic">Pathros</hi>, see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.14">Eze 29:14</reference>), which is also to be laid waste, and then names several more of the principal cities of Lower Egypt along with the chief city of Upper Egypt. צען, Egypt. <hi type="italic">Zane</hi>, Copt. <hi type="italic">Jane</hi>, is the Τανίς, <hi type="italic">Tanis</hi>, of the Greeks and Romans, on the Tanitic arm of the Nile, an ancient city of Lower Egypt; see the comm. on Num 13:22 and Isa 19:11. נא =  נא אמון in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Nah 3:8</reference>, probably “abode of Amon,” Egypt. <hi type="italic">P - amen</hi>, i.e., house of Amon, the sacred name of <hi type="italic">Thebes</hi>, the celebrated royal city of Upper Egypt, the Διὸς πόλις ἡ μεγάλη of the Greeks (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Nah 3:8</reference>). סין (literally, mire; compare the Aram. סין) is Πηλούσιον, <hi type="italic">Pelusium</hi>, which derives its name from πηλός (ὠνόμασται ἀπὸ τοῦ πηλοῦ πηλός, Strab. xvii. p. 802), because there were swamps all round. It was situated on the eastern arm of the Nile, to which it gave its name, at a distance of twenty stadia from the sea. The Egyptian name <hi type="italic">Pehromi</hi> also signifies dirty, or muddy. From this the Arabs have made <hi type="italic">Elfarama</hi>; and in the vicinity of the few ruins of the ancient Pelusium there is still a castle called Arab. <hi type="italic">t</hi>, Tineh (compare the Chaldee טינא, clay, in <reference osisRef="Dan.2.41">Dan 2:41</reference>). Ezekiel calls it the “fortress or bulwark of Egypt,” because, as Strabo (<hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>) observes, “Egypt is difficult of access here from places in the East;” for which reason Hirtius (<hi type="italic">de bell. Al. c.</hi> 27) calls it “the key of Egypt,” and Suidas (<hi type="italic">s.v.</hi>) “the key both of the entrance and exit of Egypt.” On the history of this city, see Leyrer in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Encyclopaedia</hi>. In המון נא many of the commentators find a play upon the name of the god אמון (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.25">Jer 46:25</reference>), the chief deity of Thebes, which is possible, but not very probable, as we should not expect to find a god mentioned again here after <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13">Eze 30:13</reference>; and הכרתּי would be inappropriate. - In <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.16">Eze 30:16</reference> Sin (= <hi type="italic">Pelusium</hi>) is mentioned again as the border fortress, No (= <hi type="italic">Memphis</hi>) as the capital of Upper Egypt, as all falling within the range of the judgment. The expression נף צרי יומם has caused some difficulty and given occasion to various conjectures, none of which, however, commend themselves as either simple or natural explanations.<note placement="foot">Ewald proposes to alter צרי into צדי (after the Aramaean), “rust,” and renders it: “Memphis will be eternal rust.” But to this Hitzig has very properly objected that in <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.6">Eze 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.11">Eze 24:11</reference>, rust is called חלאה; and that even in <reference osisRef="Ps.6.3">Psa 6:3</reference> יומם does not mean perpetual or eternal. Hävernick proposes to explain צרים, from the Aramaean <hi type="italic">zerâ'</hi>, to rend or tear in pieces, “Memphis shall become perpetual rents.” To this also it may be objected, that צרים in Hebrew has the standing meaning of oppressors; and that יומם, <hi type="italic">interdiu</hi>, is not equivalent to perpetual; and still further, that the preposition ל could not be omitted before צרי.</note> <div eID="gen15093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15094" type="x-p"/> As Hitzig has correctly observed, צרי יומם is the same as שׁדד בּצּהרים in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">Jer 15:8</reference>, and is the opposite of שׁדדי לילה in Oba 1:5. The enemy who comes by day, not in the night, is the enemy who does not shun open attack. The connection with נף is to be explained by the same rule as <reference osisRef="Jer.24.2">Jer 24:2</reference>, “the one basket - very good figs.” Memphis will have enemies in broad daylight, i.e., will be filled with them. און =  און, אן, in <reference osisRef="Gen.41.45">Gen 41:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.50">Gen 41:50</reference> (Egyptian <hi type="italic">An</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Anu</hi>), is the popular name of <hi type="italic">Heliopolis</hi> in Lower Egypt (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.45">Gen 41:45</reference>); and the form און (a vain thing, or idol) is probably selected intentionally in the sense of an idol-city (see the comm. on Hos 4:15), because <hi type="italic">On-Heliopolis</hi> (בּית־שׁמשׁ in <reference osisRef="Jer.43.13">Jer 43:13</reference>) was from time immemorial one of the principal seats of the Egyptian worship of the sun, and possessed a celebrated temple of the sun, with a numerous and learned priesthood (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.45">Gen 41:45</reference>, ed. 2). פּי־בסת, i.e., βουβαστός (lxx), or βουβαστίν (Herod. ii. 59), Egyptian <hi type="italic">Pi - Pasht</hi>, i.e., the place of <hi type="italic">Pasht</hi>, so called from the cat-headed <hi type="italic">Bubastis</hi> or <hi type="italic">Pasht</hi>, the Egyptian <hi type="italic">Diana</hi>, which was worshipped there in a splendid temple. It was situated on the royal canal leading to Suez, which was begun by Necho and finished under Ptolemy II, not far from its junction with the Pelusiac arm of the Nile. It was the chief seat of the <hi type="italic">Nomos Bubastites</hi>, was destroyed by the Persians, who demolished its walls (Diod. Sic. xvi. 51), and has entirely disappeared, with the exception of some heaps of ruins which still bear the name of <hi type="italic">Tel</hi> <hi type="italic">Bastah</hi>, about seven hours’ journey from the Nile (compare Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. pp. 1101ff., and Leyrer in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Encyclopaedia</hi>, <hi type="italic">s.v.</hi>). The Nomos of Bubastis, according to Herod. ii. 166, was assigned to the warrior-caste of Calasirians. The בּחוּרים, the young military men, will fall by the sword; and הנּה, not αἱ γυναῖκες (lxx and others), but the cities themselves, i.e., their civil population as distinguished from the military garrison, shall go into exile. This explanation of הנּה is commended by בּנותיה in Eze 30:18. תּחפנחס or תּחפּנחס (Jer 43:7., <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1">Eze 44:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.14">Eze 46:14</reference>), and תּחפנס in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.16">Jer 2:16</reference> (<hi type="italic">Chetib</hi>), is Τάφναι, Τάφνη (lxx), or Δάφναι (Herod. ii. 30. 107), a frontier city of Egypt in the vicinity of Pelusium, after the time of Psammetichus a fortification with a strong garrison, where a palace of Pharaoh was also to be found, according to Jer 43:9. After the destruction of Jerusalem, a portion of the Jews took refuge there, and to them Jeremiah predicted the punishment of God on the conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar (Jer 43:7., Eze 44:1.). In the case of השך the reading varies; the printed <hi type="italic">Masora</hi> at <reference osisRef="Gen.39.3">Gen 39:3</reference> giving חשׂך as the reading to be found in all the codices examined by the author of the <hi type="italic">Masora</hi>; whereas many of the codices and printed editions have חשׁך, and this is adopted in all the ancient versions. This is evidently the correct reading, as חשׂך does not furnish an appropriate meaning, and the parallel passages, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.8">Eze 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Isa 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.4">Joe 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Amo 8:9</reference>, all favour חשׁך. The darkening of the day is the phenomenal prognostic of the dawning of the great day of judgment upon the nations (cf. <reference osisRef="Joel.2.10">Joe 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.4">Joe 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.15">Joe 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Isa 13:10</reference>, etc.). This day is to dawn upon Egypt at Tachpanches, the border fortress of the land towards Syria and Palestine, when the Lord will break the yokes of Egypt. These words point back to <reference osisRef="Lev.26.13">Lev 26:13</reference>, where the deliverance of Israel from the bondage of Egypt is called the breaking in pieces of its yokes (see also <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.27">Eze 34:27</reference>). That which took place then is to be repeated here. The yokes which Egypt put upon the nations are to be broken; and all the proud might of that kingdom is to be brought to an end (גּאון עזּהּ, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.6">Eze 30:6</reference>). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.30.18">Eze 30:18</reference></hi>, היא, which stands at the head in an absolute form, points back to בּתּחפנחס. The city (<hi type="italic">Daphne</hi>) will be covered with cloud, i.e., will be overthrown by the judgment; and her daughters, i.e., the smaller cities and hamlets dependent upon her (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.46">Eze 16:46</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.6">Eze 26:6</reference>), will go into captivity in the persons of their inhabitants. It follows from this that <hi type="italic">Daphne</hi> was the chief city of a <hi type="italic">Nomos</hi> in Lower Egypt; and this is confirmed by the circumstance that there was a royal palace there. If we compare the threat in this verse, that in Tachpanches an end is to be put to the proud might of Pharaoh, with the threatening words of Jer 43:9., to the effect that Nebuchadnezzar would set up his throne at Tachpanches and smite Egypt, it is evident that the situation of Daphne must at that time have been such that the war between Egypt and Babylonia would necessarily be decided in or near this city. These prophetic utterances cannot be explained, as Kliefoth supposes, from the fact that many Jews had settled in Daphne; nor do the contents of this verse furnish any proof that Ezekiel did not utter this prophecy of his till after the Jews had settled there (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.1-Jer.43.13">Jer 43:1-13</reference> and 44). <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.19">Eze 30:19</reference> serves to round off the prophecy.
entries.55b73733172f13cfc13e819d729a136429fd0242: <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20">Eze 30:20</reference> <div eID="gen15094" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Destruction of the Might of Pharaoh by Nebuchadnezzar</title> <div sID="gen15095" type="x-p"/> According to the heading in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20">Eze 30:20</reference>, <hi type="italic">“In the eleventh year, in the first (month), on the seventh of the month, the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,”</hi> this short word of threatening against Egypt falls in the second year of the siege of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, and, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">Eze 30:21</reference> clearly shows, after the army of Pharaoh Hophra, which marched to the relief of Jerusalem, had been defeated by the Chaldeans who turned to meet it (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jer 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7">Jer 37:7</reference>). If we compare with this the date of the first prophecy against Egypt in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.1">Eze 29:1</reference>, the prophecy before us was separated from the former by an interval of three months. But as there is no allusion whatever in Ezekiel 29 to Pharaoh’s attempt to come to the relief of the besieged city of Jerusalem, or to his repulse, the arrival of the Egyptian army in Palestine, its defeat, and its repulse by the Chaldeans, seems to have occurred in the interval between these two prophecies, towards the close of the tenth year.
entries.d8ba0ceb43ecf39a8f4ad4a817af9e1fedcf8554: <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21-Ezek.30.26">Eze 30:21-26</reference> <div eID="gen15095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15096" type="x-p"/> Eze 30:21. <hi type="italic">son of man, the arm of Pharaoh the king of Egypt have I broken; and, behold, it will no more be bound up, to apply remedies, to put on a bandage to bind it up, that it may grow strong to grasp the sword.</hi> Eze 30:22. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Behold, I will deal with Pharaoh the king of Egypt, and will break both his arms, the strong one and the broken one, and will cause the sword to fall out of his hand.</hi> Eze 30:23. <hi type="italic">And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them in the lands,</hi> Eze 30:24. <hi type="italic">And will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and give my sword into his hand, and will break the arms of Pharaoh, so that he shall groan the groanings of a pierced one before him.</hi> Eze 30:25. <hi type="italic">I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharaoh will fall; and they shall know that I am Jehovah, when I give my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, that he may stretch it against the land of Egypt.</hi> Eze 30:26. <hi type="italic">I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them in the lands; and they shall know that I am Jehovah.</hi> - The perfect שׁברתּי in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">Eze 30:21</reference> is not a prophetic utterance of the certainty of the future, but a pure preterite. This may be seen “both from the allusion in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">Eze 30:21</reference></hi> to the condition resulting from the shbr שׁבר, and also to the obviously antithetical relation of <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.22">Eze 30:22</reference>, in which future events are predicted” (Hitzig). The arm is a figurative expression for power, here for military power, as it wields the sword. God broke the arm of Pharaoh by the defeat which the Chaldeans inflicted upon Pharaoh Hophra, when he was marching to the relief of besieged Jerusalem. חבּשׁה is a present, as is apparent from the infinitive clauses ('לתת וגו) which follow, altogether apart from הנּה; and חבשׁ signifies to bind up, for the purpose of healing a broken limb, that remedies may be applied and a bandage put on. לחזקהּ, that it may become strong or sound, is subordinate to the preceding clause, and governs the infinitive which follows. The fact that the further judgment which is to fall upon Pharaoh is introduced with לכן (therefore) here (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.22">Eze 30:22</reference>), notwithstanding the fact that it has not been preceded by any enumeration of the guilt which occasioned it, may be accounted for on the ground that the causal לכן forms a link with the concluding clause of <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">Eze 30:21</reference> : the arm shall not be healed, so as to be able to grasp or hold the sword. Because Pharaoh is not to attain any more to victorious power, therefore God will shatter both of his arms, the strong, i.e., the sound one and the broken one, that is to say, will smite it so completely, that the sword will fall from his hand. The Egyptians are to be scattered among the nations, as is repeated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.23">Eze 30:23</reference> <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> from Eze 29:12. God will give the sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and equip and strengthen him to destroy the might of Pharaoh, that the latter may groan before him like one who is pierced with the sword. This thought is repeated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.25">Eze 30:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.26">Eze 30:26</reference> with an intimation of the purpose of this divine procedure. That purpose it: that men may come to recognise Jehovah as God the Lord. The subject to וידעוּ is indefinite; and the rendering of the lxx is a very good one, καὶ γνώσονται πάντες.  <chapter eID="Ezek.30"/> <div eID="gen15096" type="x-p"/>
